source_read: Publisher HTML (The Lancet Global Health, open access), reached through the DOI link; page title confirmed in my own tab; the corrected online version of 25 January 2017. Whole text read with get_page_text (53,190 characters, complete): Summary, Introduction, Research in context panel, Methods, Results, the Table (as text), Discussion, contributors, declaration of interests, acknowledgments and reference list. Figures 1 and 3 (flow charts) read on screen, enlarged; Figures 2 and 4 (maps) looked at, no values taken. Correction notice read (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e276). For the card check only, PROSPERO records CRD42016033835 and CRD42016033837 were read at the stated place. Supplementary appendix (PDF) not read.

claims.note: This source supports only the dating sentence. The review says FAS was 'first described in 1973', and its FAS search starts on 1 November 1973, 'when FAS was first described'. Both statements cite reference 13, Jones KL and Smith DW, 'Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy', Lancet 1973;302:999-1001: two of the authors, with the name in the title, as the claim says. For context only (registry, not the paper): the same team's PROSPERO record for the FAS/FASD review (CRD42016033837) dates the first description to January 1973.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Methods > Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd paragraph; References, 13
anchors.extracted: FAS said to be first described in 1973 (ref 13); the FAS search covers studies from 1 November 1973 (when FAS was first described, ref 13) to 30 June 2015. Ref 13: Jones KL, Smith DW, Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy, Lancet 1973;302:999-1001.

claims.overstatement: None for this source's part. The claim frames the FAS figures as model estimates, as it should. The Abel definition of heavy drinking (two or more drinks a day, or five to six per occasion) is a cited study's definition, not advice.
claims.note: All Popova numbers in the statement and magnitude match the source: 62 studies from 19 countries; FAS 14.6 per 10,000 (9.4-23.3) and the six regional figures (Table); the five highest countries with their intervals and prediction flags; quotient of 1 in 67 from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA; about 119,000 a year from 81,536,534 live births; Abel's 4.3%; FAS:FASD of about 1 to 9 or 10; meta-analysis for 7 countries and the quotient for 180; funding by the authors' institute with no external funding sought; no competing interests. Recomputed: 14.6 per 10,000 = 1.46 per 1,000 (1.5); 9.8% / 67 = 14.63 per 10,000; 67 / 13 = 5.15; 14.6 per 10,000 x 81,536,534 = 119,043; 1 / 0.043 = 23 (the paper's 1 in 23), 67 / 23 = 2.9 (its 'about three times'). Four qualifiers the claim could carry. (1) No FAS study came from the Eastern Mediterranean or South-East Asia regions: Figure 3 gives 9 African, 27 Americas, 18 European and 8 Western Pacific studies, and the text says four regions. Those two regional FAS figures (0.2 and 2.7) are therefore entirely the predicted drinking prevalence divided by 67. (2) Of the 62 studies, 22 used active case ascertainment, 20 passive surveillance, 14 were clinic-based and 6 used mixed methods. The primary analysis kept only active-ascertainment and clinic studies with a stated definition, and adding the others lowered the estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA (appendix). (3) South Africa has the highest, meta-analysed estimate (585.3) but is not among the seven quotient countries, and the main text does not name the seven meta-analysed countries. (4) The 119,000 applies a prevalence per 10,000 people to live births; the Research in context panel restates it per 10,000 live births. A question for the senior author, using outside data and not checkable from the source: if South Africa's meta-analysed 585.3 entered the birth-weighted African average, that average (14.8, almost exactly 10.0% / 67) could hold only if South Africa carried well under 1% of the region's weighted births. Its real share is several times that, so the regional figure may not include the meta-analysed value. Appendix table A7 would settle it.

anchors.extracted: FAS search: 11,110 records, 62 studies retained, data from 19 countries in four WHO regions (African, Americas, European, Western Pacific). Global FAS 14.6 per 10,000 people (9.4-23.3). Pooled by random-effects meta-analysis for 7 countries; for 180 countries, the quotient of women who drank in pregnancy per FAS case applied to drinking prevalence. Quotient: 1 in 67 mothers who drank, from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA; about 119,000 children with FAS a year from 81,536,534 live births (latest year 2000-14).

FAS per 10,000, 2012, weighted by live births: African 14.8 (8.9-21.5); Americas 16.6 (11.0-24.0); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2-0.9); European 37.4 (24.7-54.2); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3-8.1); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7-19.4); worldwide 14.6 (9.4-23.3). Each regional figure is within rounding of that region's drinking prevalence divided by 67 (editors' arithmetic).

Five highest FAS countries per 10,000: Belarus 69.1 (42.1-103.5; prediction), Italy 82.1 (42.1-134.6), Ireland 89.7 (50.4-142.8; prediction), Croatia 115.2 (34.8-236.0), South Africa 585.3 (430.7-761.7); five lowest below 0.05 (prediction): Oman, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait. European region highest (37.4), Eastern Mediterranean lowest (0.2).

anchors.locator: Figure 3; Results, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Methods > Meta-analyses, 5th and 6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Figure 3: 62 FAS studies by region: African 9, Americas 27, European 18, Western Pacific 8; none from the Eastern Mediterranean or South-East Asia. 22 active case ascertainment, 20 passive surveillance, 14 clinic-based, 6 mixed; 40 with an established guideline or case definition. Primary analysis: active ascertainment or clinic-based with a stated definition; the secondary analysis adding passive surveillance and undefined cases gave lower estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA (appendix p 36). Quotient method: average women who drank per FAS case in countries with data, applied to each country's drinking prevalence; Monte Carlo intervals (1,000,000 samples).

Abel (1995): 4.3% of children born to heavy-drinking pregnant women (average two or more drinks a day, or five to six per occasion; no drink size given) have FAS, i.e. 1 in 23, about three times the general-population quotient. The FAS-to-FASD ratio is believed to be about 1 to 9 or 10 (Chudley 2008). FAS is much higher in some populations (Indigenous Australian 92.6 per 10,000).

Limitations: self-reported drinking may be under-reported, so drinking and FAS prevalence may be underestimated; quantity and frequency not analysed (not reported or inconsistent); FAS diagnostic guidelines unspecified or inconsistent, with diagnosis unreliable across systems; predictions carry measurement error and omit variables such as alcohol policies; FAS studies mostly regionally confined to areas where high prevalence was expected; WHO member states only.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim separates measured from modelled figures and avoids the paper's 'alarmingly'; no drink size or amount is given, and nothing reads as advice.
claims.note: Every number matches the source: studies published 1 January 1984 to 30 June 2014; 328 studies, 50 countries; 9.8% (8.9-11.1) worldwide; the six regional figures with intervals (Table); five highest countries all in the European region (Ireland 60.4%, 42.8-76.8, the top), with the UK's upper limit misprinted ('49.%'); five countries at 0%, all by prediction; 29 countries pooled, 158 predicted from GDP per capita (purchasing power parity), women's mean total alcohol consumption and WHO region; predictions for 2012 and live-birth weighting. Reference groups are not applicable (prevalence). Recomputed: 29 + 158 = 187; 50 - 29 = 21 countries with data given a prediction (those with one study, or an interval of 0-100%), as the claim says; about 10 in 100 and about 25 in 100 are fair roundings. One qualifier worth adding: Figure 1 counts only one study each from the Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia regions (25 African, 137 Americas, 1 Eastern Mediterranean, 121 European, 1 South-East Asia, 45 Western Pacific; 330 study-country entries for 328 studies). Under the paper's rule a single-study country receives a prediction, so the 0.2% and 1.8% regional figures are in effect wholly modelled, and the data come mostly from the Americas and Europe (258 of 330 entries). The exclusion list also named women of low socioeconomic status and women with HIV, and preference went to estimates after pregnancy recognition, over the whole pregnancy, within 6 weeks after birth, or by a validated method.

anchors.extracted: 23,470 records, 328 studies retained; general-population data on drinking in pregnancy from 50 countries in all six WHO regions; global prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy 9.8% (95% CI 8.9-11.1).

Any alcohol use during pregnancy, general population, 2012, weighted by live births: African 10.0% (8.5-11.8); Americas 11.2% (9.4-12.6); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1-0.9); European 25.2% (21.6-29.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9-5.1); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5-11.6); worldwide 9.8% (8.9-11.1).

Random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries, fractional response modelling for 158 with one or no study. Highest: Russia 36.5% (18.7-56.4), UK 41.3% (32.9 to an incomplete upper limit), Denmark 45.8% (30.9-61.2), Belarus 46.6% (42.4-50.7; prediction), Ireland 60.4% (42.8-76.8), all European region. 0% (prediction) in Oman, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait. Heterogeneity and publication-bias tests only in the appendix.

anchors.locator: Methods > Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph; Methods > Meta-analyses, 2nd, 3rd and 7th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Search 1 January 1984 to 30 June 2014. Excluded: studies excluding abstainers, special populations (Indigenous women, adolescents, low socioeconomic status, HIV, alcohol use disorder), pooled estimates, duplicates. Preference for estimates after pregnancy recognition, whole pregnancy, within 6 weeks post partum, or validated method. Countries with one or no study (or a 0-100% interval) predicted by fractional response regression on GDP per capita (purchasing power parity), women's mean total alcohol consumption and WHO region (European and Americas regions split by income); predictions for 2012; regional and global averages weighted by live births (latest year 2000-14); Monte Carlo intervals.

Flow chart: 23,433 database + 37 other records = 23,470; 11,248 duplicates; 12,222 screened; 766 full texts; 438 excluded (267 irrelevant data, 146 unrepresentative samples, 14 duplicate publication, 11 excluded abstainers); final box 330 eligible study entries: African 25, Americas 137, Eastern Mediterranean 1, European 121, South-East Asia 1, Western Pacific 45 (some studies cover more than one country or year).

Drinking in pregnancy is reported much higher in some at-risk groups (Inuit women in northern Quebec 60.5%, over ten times the Canadian general-population estimate). Limitations: some studies non-representative or with unvalidated tools; self-report may under-report, so prevalence may be underestimated; frequency and quantity not analysed; predictions may diverge from true values; WHO member states only.

reporting_issues.note: A likely resolution: 3191 per 10,000 is a misprint for 319.1 per 10,000 (31.9 per 1,000). That fits the stated 'more than 14 times' (319.1 / 14 = 23 per 10,000, a plausible Brazilian general-population figure beside the Americas' 16.6) and sits below the companion paper's FASD figure for the same orphanage (170.2 per 1,000). Still to be checked against the primary study.

Checked in both PROSPERO records. One nuance: the FAS record's planned split by ascertainment (active or clinic-based vs any method) was carried out, as the primary and secondary analyses. The dropped ascertainment-method subgroups are those of the drinking record (self-report, meconium, other biomarkers).

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from items 2 (registered on 31 January 2016, after the searches closed; confirmed in both records) and 7 (no list of excluded studies in the article) alone. Items 11 and 15 are arguable for a prevalence review, but changing them would not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One more point: the Discussion explains South Africa's high FAS prevalence by a binge pattern it calls 'a direct cause of FAS', using regional per-capita figures, not data from this review.

missed: Study counts by region (Figures 1 and 3), which matter for any claim about regional figures. Drinking: 25 African, 137 Americas, 1 Eastern Mediterranean, 121 European, 1 South-East Asia and 45 Western Pacific entries, so the Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia drinking estimates rest on one study each and are in effect modelled. FAS: 9, 27, 18 and 8 studies, none in those two regions. Figure 1's final box says 330 studies against 328 in the text (entries by country or year). Both flow charts label the title-and-abstract exclusions as 'excluded after full-text screening' (trivial).

Registry dates differ from the paper. The drinking record's search window starts in January 1983 (paper: 1 January 1984), and the FAS/FASD record dates the first description of FAS to January 1973 (paper: 1 November 1973). Neither difference is explained.

A question needing outside data (live births by country, not in the paper). The regional and global FAS figures match drinking prevalence divided by 67 almost exactly (key finding 7). If South Africa's meta-analysed 585.3 per 10,000 had entered the birth-weighted African average, that average would sit well above 10.0% / 67 = 14.9, unless South Africa carried well under 1% of the region's weighted births. So the regional and global averages may not include the meta-analysed country values. Appendix table A7 would settle it.
